newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Markets cautious over new Austrian finmin.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Markets cautious over new Austrian finmin.

text.p: Austrian markets and analysts reacted with caution on Friday to the appoinment of Rudolf Edlinger as the country's finance minister-designate, saying the Vienna City finance councillor was little known in business circles.
Edlinger, 56, was chosen by chancellor-in-waiting Viktor Klima on Friday after outgoing chancellor Franz Vranitzky named incumbent finance minister Klima as his successor.

Market sources had widely expected Klima to choose an expert outsider rather than a professional politician as his new finance minister to steer Austria into European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

"Very little is known about him," a London-based Austria analyst told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity. "But in any case, he's a political heavyweight and not the kind of expert minister that the business community had hoped for."

Social Democrat Edlinger, 56, has served as the City of Vienna's finance councillor since November 1994. He has borne responsibility for Austria's biggest regional budget, with annual expenditure of around 134 billion schillings ($11.68 billion).
"I will dedicate the necessary energy to this tough job. I will take it on with optimism," Edlinger told Austrian radio in reaction to his appointment.

Edlinger's most pressing task will be to make sure that Austria makes the grade for a single European currency. Negotiations over the country's two-year budget for 1998 and 1999 budget are expected to start in the spring.

Edlinger, a professional lithographer, was a key player in a political team that two weeks ago hammered out a coalition deal over the sale of Austria's most famous bank Creditanstalt to market leader Bank Austria.
The heavy-set smoker had insisted earlier this week that he was not a candidate to take over the finance portfolio and had set his sights on retirement by the year 2000.
"It's a bit surprising that he's now agreed to it even though he just recently said he wasn't going to do it," a Vienna-based analyst said.
Stock and bond markets showed little interest in the new man.
The ATX index of 21 blue chips was down almost 0.5 percent in the last half hour of trading in Vienna after languishing for most of the day. The Austrian bond future was down 33 points at 108.15.
"We're certaintly not going to jump for joy," said one analyst at a Vienna bank.
